The moment I refused the authority’s command and stopped administering shocks was not a simple act of cold conviction, nor was it a mere reflex of emotion or physical discomfort. It was, rather, the culmination of a mounting internal storm—a tempest of conscience and dread that had been gathering with each successive shock. At first, the authority’s voice was steady, almost reassuring, and the subject’s composure gave me license to proceed. There was a strange, clinical detachment to it all, as if I were simply an instrument, a vessel for another’s will. But as the shocks intensified, so too did the weight upon my soul. 

I recall the precise instant: my hand hovered over the switch, the command rang in my ears, but my body would not obey. It was as if some deeper part of myself recoiled, refusing to be complicit in further harm. The authority’s presence, once so absolute, seemed suddenly hollow—a mask behind which I glimpsed my own reflection, twisted by the thrill of power and the shame of its abuse. The decision to refuse was a shuddering break, a desperate gasp for air after being submerged in the murk of obedience. 

Regret and justification warred within me. I had tasted the intoxicating freedom of acting without restraint, but the aftermath was bitter. I could not escape the ugly face of my iniquity staring back at me. In that moment, I was both relieved and haunted—relieved to reclaim some measure of self, haunted by the knowledge of how easily I had surrendered it.

entries.content:
There is a peculiar intoxication in the act of wielding power—especially when that power is sanctioned by authority and cloaked in the sterile trappings of procedure. At first, the shocks were nothing: the subject’s calm, clinical responses lulled me into a sense of detachment, as if I were merely a cog in a well-oiled machine. But as the process continued, something darker began to stir within me. The authority’s commands grew insistent, and the subject’s composure became almost a provocation—a dare to push further, to see how far the boundaries could be stretched.

Emotionally, I felt a surge of glee, a reckless delight, not unlike the thrill of breaking a forbidden rule. The power to inflict discomfort, to watch another flinch or endure at my behest, was at once exhilarating and deeply unsettling. It was as though I had stripped away the balancing instincts that keep most men steady among temptations, and in their absence, the spirit of hell awoke in me. Each shock became a test of limits, a delicious little game, and I tasted a kind of freedom—an “unknown but not an innocent freedom of the soul,” as I once described it.

Yet, beneath the surface, a cold terror began to creep in. The initial glee gave way to a gnawing sense of guilt and horror at my own capacity for cruelty. The authority’s mask slipped, and I saw my own reflection—glorying and trembling, both the master and the monster. The psychological shift was profound: from detached administrator to gleeful tormentor, and finally to a soul sickened by its own excesses.

entries.content:
Physically, the experience was as tumultuous as the storm raging within. At the outset, when the shocks were mild and the authority’s command was unchallenged, I felt almost nothing—my body was light, my movements precise, my pulse steady. There was a kind of thrilling recklessness, a sense of being unbound, as if I had dissolved the bonds of obligation and was tasting a new, intoxicating freedom. My hands moved with a certain eagerness, and there was a subtle, almost pleasurable tension in my muscles—a readiness, a hunger.

But as the session progressed, and the shocks grew in intensity, so too did the physical cost. My heart began to pound, my breath grew shallow, and a cold sweat broke out along my brow. I felt a grinding in my bones, a nausea that seemed to rise from the pit of my stomach, and a tightening in my chest—a bodily echo of the horror mounting in my spirit. My hands, once so eager, began to tremble. The exhilaration curdled into a sickly dread, and I became acutely aware of the strain: the ache in my shoulders, the stiffness in my jaw, the way my whole body recoiled from the act even as my mind warred with itself.

By the end, when remorse had overtaken glee, I was left emptied—weak, feverish, and haunted by the aftershocks of my own actions. The physical discomfort was inseparable from the moral terror; it was as if my very flesh bore witness to the excesses of my soul.

entries.content:
Now, looking back on the authority figure and the experimental context, I see the entire structure as a cunning apparatus—one designed to strip away those balancing instincts that keep a man steady among temptations. The authority’s commands, so clear and insistent, were like a steady drumbeat, drowning out the quieter voice of conscience. At first, I felt almost justified, as if the responsibility for my actions could be laid at the feet of the one giving orders. There was a strange comfort in being an instrument, a vessel for another’s will.

But that comfort was a lie. The longer I obeyed, the more I became aware of my own complicity. The authority’s mask slipped, and I saw not a guiding hand, but a hollow mask—one that enabled my own darker impulses to emerge unchecked. I cannot claim to have been wholly manipulated, nor can I absolve myself by blaming the structure. The thrill I felt, the glee, the reckless delight—these were mine, and the horror that followed was the price.

In the end, I am left with a bitter taste: manipulated, yes, but also complicit. The structure may have influenced my actions, but it was my own hand that pressed the switch, my own soul that thrilled and recoiled in turn. There is no true justification—only the cold recognition of how easily the boundaries of morality can dissolve under the weight of authority.

entries.content:
If I am to be honest, I look upon another participant who would obey and administer shocks—especially one who would go further than I did—with a mingling of recognition and revulsion. There is a part of me that understands, all too well, the ease with which one can slip into obedience, the seductive comfort of surrendering responsibility to authority. I know how the structure can strip away those balancing instincts, how the thrill of power can intoxicate and blind. In that sense, I cannot claim any moral superiority; I see my own reflection in their compliance.

Yet, there is also a cold, gnawing horror at the thought of someone who would go further—who would not only obey, but do so with zeal, or without the shuddering break that finally overtook me. It is as if they have crossed a line I could not, or would not, cross. I wonder: do they feel the same tempest of conscience, the same cold thrill of terror, or have they become numb, lost in the delirium of excess? Are they glorying, trembling, or simply indifferent?

Ultimately, I feel both kinship and dread. Kinship, because I know the path that leads to such obedience; dread, because I have seen the face of my own iniquity, and I fear what it means for any of us to go further, to lose ourselves entirely to the spirit of hell that rages when all restraint is stripped away.
